unitTitle: Advanced Front-End Technologies (CSS animations, transforms, custom properties, JS async/await, APIs, fetch, JSON, Form Handling, Client-Side Security)

lessons.title: CSS Custom Properties
lessons.description: Storing reusable values in CSS variables, theming a page, and changing variables from JavaScript.
hints: Custom property names start with two hyphens, e.g. --brand-colour: #00695c;
Use a custom property with var(), e.g. color: var(--brand-colour);
Declare custom properties on :root to make them available to every element on the page.
Change a custom property from JavaScript with document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--brand-colour', '#283593');

lessons.title: Transforms and Transitions
lessons.description: Moving, rotating and scaling elements, and animating changes smoothly with transitions.
hints: Several transforms go in one declaration, separated by spaces: transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.05); A second transform declaration replaces the first.
Put the transition on the element's normal state, not only on :hover, so it animates both ways.
Transitions on transform and opacity are the smoothest, because the browser does not need to recalculate the layout.
Add :focus-visible alongside :hover, so keyboard users see the same effect.

lessons.title: CSS Animations
lessons.description: Creating animations with keyframes, using motion with purpose, and respecting reduced motion settings.
hints: The name after @keyframes must match the animation-name exactly.
The animation shorthand takes the name, duration, timing function and number of repeats, e.g. animation: spin 1s linear infinite;
animation-fill-mode: forwards; keeps the element in its final state when the animation ends.
Wrap motion you want to turn off in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { ... }

lessons.title: JSON and Local Storage
lessons.description: Converting data to and from JSON, and saving it in the browser so it is remembered between visits.
hints: Local storage only stores strings. Use JSON.stringify() before saving an array or object, and JSON.parse() after reading it.
getItem() returns null when nothing has been saved yet, so always have a default value ready.
In JSON, property names and strings must use double quotes, and there can be no comma after the last item.
In this platform, each lesson's storage is kept separate, so saving data here cannot affect the platform or other lessons.

lessons.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
lessons.description: Understanding code that waits, using promises, async and await, and handling failures with try and catch.
hints: await only works inside a function declared with async.
An async function always returns a promise, even if it returns a simple value.
Put code that could fail inside try { ... }, and decide what the user should see in catch { ... }.
Code after an await waits for it to finish, but code outside the async function carries on straight away.

lessons.title: Fetching Data
lessons.description: Loading data with fetch, checking the response, and showing loading and failure states on the page.
hints: Check response.ok before using the data. A response can arrive successfully but still say the request failed, such as a 404.
response.json() also needs await, because reading the data takes time too.
Show a loading message before calling fetch, then replace it with the results or a failure message.
To test your failure message, temporarily change the file name in the fetch call to one that does not exist.

lessons.title: Working With APIs
lessons.description: Reading API documentation, building requests with query parameters, and choosing a suitable public API.
hints: Copy the endpoint address from the API's documentation exactly, including https://.
Build query strings with URLSearchParams, so that spaces and special characters are encoded correctly.
A suitable API for the browser needs no key, uses HTTPS, and supports CORS. Test it by fetching it from the preview.
Do not send a request on every key press. Fetch when the user submits a search, to stay within the API's rate limits.

lessons.title: Displaying API Data
lessons.description: Rendering fetched data, filtering and sorting it, and handling empty or unexpected results.
hints: Log the API's response first, to see exactly what shape the data has before writing code to display it.
Provide a fallback for missing values with ??, e.g. item.name ?? "Unknown".
Sort a copy of the array, not the original: [...items].sort(...). Use a.name.localeCompare(b.name) for text and a.value - b.value for numbers.
When a search returns an empty array, show a clear message instead of an empty space.

lessons.title: Form Handling and Validation
lessons.description: Handling form submissions with JavaScript, validating realistic input, and showing accessible error messages.
hints: Listen for the form's submit event, not the button's click, and call event.preventDefault() first.
Trim every value before checking it, so that a field containing only spaces counts as empty.
Check each field for what could realistically go wrong: missing, the wrong format, too short or too long.
Link each error message to its field with aria-describedby, and set aria-invalid="true" on the field.

lessons.title: Dialogs and Form Feedback
lessons.description: Building accessible modal dialogs, managing focus, and giving clear feedback after a form is submitted.
hints: dialog.showModal() opens a dialog as a modal, and dialog.close() closes it.
Pressing Escape closes a modal dialog automatically, so you do not need to code it yourself.
When a dialog closes, move focus back to the button that opened it.
Announce a success message with an element that has aria-live="polite", so screen reader users hear it.

lessons.title: Client-Side Security
lessons.description: Protecting users from common front-end risks, and understanding the vulnerabilities of database-driven applications.
hints: Display user input and API data with textContent, never innerHTML.
Client-side validation helps users, but anyone can bypass it. A server must always check the data again.
Never put API keys, passwords or other secrets in front-end code: anyone can read it in the browser.
Add integrity and crossorigin attributes to scripts loaded from a CDN, so the browser rejects them if they have been changed.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Build an API-Powered Page
lessons.description: Build a page that fetches, displays, filters and sorts API data, with a validated form, a details dialog and purposeful animation.
hints: Build one feature at a time, and check it works before starting the next.
Log the API's response with console.log before writing the code that displays it.
Test what happens when the request fails, by temporarily changing the address to one that does not exist.
Test the page in both a narrow pop-out preview and the fullscreen preview.
